voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.

beats.vo: Late November, twenty twenty-two. DoorDash drivers started showing up at Smoque BBQ in Chicago, to pick up orders the kitchen had never received. Four or five of them.
Co-owner Barry Sorkin went on the app. There was a Smoque storefront. Same hours. Same address. Similar food. It was fake.
It had happened in October, too: a duplicate page beside the real one, with Smoque's menu copied. This time, co-owner Mike McDermott said, the new storefront was up, and theirs was gone.
How the real page was taken down, he said, wasn't clear. Customers ordered, and paid. The kitchen never saw the orders. Where that money went wasn't clear either.

Smoque told customers to stop ordering through DoorDash. Within a day, the fake page was down. DoorDash said it would reimburse the customers, and Smoque. It said it checks tax information, and can ask for ID.
To prove he was the real owner, Sorkin had to send DoorDash a lot of paperwork. His question: how did someone set up a storefront with his restaurant's name on it, without those steps?
